approachQuestion.prompt:
Standing for each submission

For each score, return its dense standing in the ORIGINAL input order: the highest distinct score has standing 1, the next distinct score has standing 2, and so on. Equal scores share a standing. Do not modify the caller’s scores. Return an array of n standings.

Constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 200,000; −1,000,000,000 ≤ scores[i] ≤ 1,000,000,000. Scores are opaque comparison keys; hashing, radix, counting and bucket structures are excluded.

Examples: [40,90,40,70] → [3,1,3,2]. [5,5,5] → [1,1,1].

Choose the most efficient valid method among these options under the stated model; avoid removable repeated work.
constraints: The complete input/output and mutation contract in the prompt applies to every option.

options.text: Create (score, originalIndex) records, sort by score descending, increase a standing only when the score changes, and write each standing to its originalIndex in the result.
options.feedback: The sorted traversal identifies distinct score groups while the stored index restores each result to its caller-visible position.

options.text: Sort a copy descending and return the standings in that sorted order.
options.feedback: The output positions are wrong: [40,90,40,70] needs [3,1,3,2], not [1,2,3,3].

options.text: Sort indexed records descending and assign standing equal to sorted position plus one.
options.feedback: This gives tied entries different standings: [5,5,5] must produce [1,1,1].

options.text: For each original score, scan all scores into a temporary distinct list using linear membership checks, retain only larger scores, and return that list’s length plus one.
options.feedback: Counting distinct larger scores is correct, but rebuilding those lists and scanning them for membership adds avoidable repeated work.

feedback.reason: Dense standing increments once per distinct score group, not once per submission.
details: Create indexed records, comparison merge sort them by descending score, scan equal-score groups and scatter each group’s dense standing to the saved original indices.
Dense standing increments once per distinct score group, not once per submission. Saved original indices let the sorted group receive one standing and scatter it back into the requested input order.

“Create (score, originalIndex) records, sort by score descending, increase a standing only when the score changes, and write each standing to its originalIndex in the result.”: The sorted traversal identifies distinct score groups while the stored index restores each result to its caller-visible position.
“Sort a copy descending and return the standings in that sorted order.”: The output positions are wrong: [40,90,40,70] needs [3,1,3,2], not [1,2,3,3].
“Sort indexed records descending and assign standing equal to sorted position plus one.”: This gives tied entries different standings: [5,5,5] must produce [1,1,1].

“For each original score, scan all scores into a temporary distinct list using linear membership checks, retain only larger scores, and return that list’s length plus one.”: Counting distinct larger scores is correct, but rebuilding those lists and scanning them for membership adds avoidable repeated work.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze only the revealed method using conventional comparison merge sort with a linear merge buffer and a logarithmic recursion stack. Choose the tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space bounds in n. Count all working copies, indexed records, buffers and stack frames; exclude the caller input and returned output. No hashing is used. Comparisons, arithmetic, record copies and array accesses take constant time; preallocate output capacity so no resizing assumption is needed.

options.text: O(n log n) time, O(n) additional space
O(n log n) time, O(1) additional space

feedback.reason: Sort indexed scores, group ties, and scatter each standing once.
details: Sorting dominates the linear scan: O(n log n) worst-case time. The merge buffer and copied/indexed records use O(n) auxiliary memory; the O(log n) recursion stack does not change this total. The output is excluded. The quadratic-time option overstates the tight bound, constant space omits the buffer, and linear time omits comparison sorting.
